young.html: Bertrand Russell was an English thinker who liked to start with very ordinary things, like the kitchen table, and ask very hard questions about them.

Look at a table. What color is it? It looks brown, but where the light shines it looks almost white, and in the shadows nearly black. Walk around it and its shape seems to change too: a rectangle from above, a slanted shape from the side. So which is the real table? The one you see, or something behind what you see?

young.name: gb-russell-table
young.cap: Move around the table and move the lamp. Watch how its shape and shine seem to change, while the table itself stays the same.

young.html: A changing coin. Hold a coin flat in front of you and look straight down: it is a circle. Now tilt it slowly. What shape do you see? Draw three shapes the coin made. Is the coin still round?

full.html: Bertrand Russell (1872–1970) was a mathematician and philosopher at Cambridge. With Alfred North Whitehead he wrote Principia Mathematica (1910–13), which tried to build mathematics from logic. The Problems of Philosophy (1912) was a small book for a popular series, the Home University Library. It is still one of the most widely read introductions to philosophy. Russell won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1950.

full.text: Is there any knowledge in the world which is so certain that no reasonable man could doubt it?
full.author: Bertrand Russell
full.work: The Problems of Philosophy, Chapter I
full.ed: Williams and Norgate, London (Home University Library)

full.html: Russell's first example is his table. Its color, shape and feel change with the light, the angle and the person. He concludes:

full.text: It is evident from what we have found, that there is no colour which pre-eminently appears to be the colour of the table, or even of any one particular part of the table—it appears to be of different colours from different points of view.
full.author: Bertrand Russell
full.work: The Problems of Philosophy, Chapter I
full.ed: Williams and Norgate, London (Home University Library)

full.html: What we directly know, Russell says, are sense-data: the colors, shapes and sounds we are aware of. The table itself, if it exists, is something we infer. He admits we cannot prove there is a world beyond our sense-data, but our "instinctive belief" in it is the simplest way to explain what we experience, so it is reasonable to accept it.

full.name: gb-russell-table
full.cap: The same table from different places and in different light.

full.html: Russell separates knowledge by acquaintance, direct awareness of something (this patch of color, this feeling), from knowledge by description, knowing something as "the so-and-so" (the first emperor of Rome, the center of the earth). Most of what we know about the world, and all we know of other times and places, is by description.

Why do we expect the sun to rise tomorrow? Because it always has. But a past pattern does not prove a future one. Russell's example is the chicken that is fed every day, and so expects food each morning, until one day the farmer comes for it instead. Inductive reasoning makes conclusions probable, never certain; and, Russell argues, the principle of induction itself cannot be proved from experience without arguing in a circle.

full.title: An inductive argument, tested
full.q: Every swan I have ever seen is white. So all swans are white. Is this argument deductive or inductive, and could the conclusion be false even if the premise is true?
steps: The premise reports past observations; the conclusion reaches beyond them to all swans.
That is inductive reasoning: it can make a conclusion more probable, but not certain.
Black swans were in fact found in Australia by European explorers in 1697.
full.a: Inductive; yes, the conclusion can be false (and was).

full.text: Truth, and the value of philosophy

full.html: A belief is true, Russell says, when it corresponds to a fact, and false when it does not. Truth depends on the world, not on whether a belief is useful, a direct reply to William James's pragmatism. The book ends with the value of philosophy itself:

full.text: Philosophy is to be studied, not for the sake of any definite answers to its questions, since no definite answers can, as a rule, be known to be true, but rather for the sake of the questions themselves; because these questions enlarge our conception of what is possible, enrich our intellectual imagination, and diminish the dogmatic assurance which closes the mind against speculation.
full.author: Bertrand Russell
full.work: The Problems of Philosophy, Chapter XV
full.ed: Williams and Norgate, London (Home University Library)

full.html: Russell later changed many of his views, and philosophers have challenged the idea of sense-data as the things we directly see; many now say we see tables, not data about tables. But the book's questions, about appearance and reality, induction, and truth, remain the standard starting points of the subject.
Thinking Russell said the table is not real. He said our belief in it is reasonable but cannot be proved, and that we know it through its appearances.

items: Descartes' Meditations, on the 17th-century part of this ladder, also began with doubt; Russell discusses him in Chapter II.
Berkeley argued that there is nothing behind the appearances; Russell's Chapter IV answers him.
Hume first raised the problem of induction; Russell's Chapter VI restates it.
James's Pragmatism, the rung before Bergson, defined truth by what works; Russell defined it by correspondence with fact.
Wittgenstein, Russell's student, later questioned how words connect to the world at all.
How do you know the world exists when you are not looking?
Can we ever be certain the future will be like the past?
Is a belief true because it matches the facts, or because it works?
What is the use of a question that has no final answer?

questions: Pick an object in the room. How does it look different from where each of you sits?
Why does the sun rising every day make you expect it tomorrow? Is that a good reason?
Name something you know by acquaintance and something you know only by description.
Russell said philosophy is worth it for the questions, not the answers. Do you agree?
Have you ever been sure of something and found you were wrong? What did you learn?
